clue.text: Worms regularly found next to pillar inside no-frills recycling facility

indicators.note: whatever is inside sits within the walls of a larger word

parts.note: something with no frills is basic and inexpensive

indicators.note: placing one thing beside another means the two runs of letters simply join up
doing something regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: the second and fourth letters
a post is an upright pole or pillar

explanation.surface: A bare-bones recycling depot where worms turn up beside a pillar.
explanation.walkthrough: The worms really belong in a compost scene, which is why they are easy to take literally; 'no-frills' is the outer word that is split open.
explanation.definitionFit: A garden pile of rotting vegetable matter turns kitchen and garden waste back into soil, a homely kind of recycling.

clue.text: Rackets created by accountant with company fraudsters

indicators.note: going with something means being joined to it, so the pieces sit side by side

parts.note: CA is a chartered accountant
the standard abbreviation for company
phonies are fakes or frauds

explanation.surface: Crooked schemes run by an accountant working with a firm of swindlers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rackets' reads as criminal scams, which the accountant and fraudsters encourage; here it means loud noises.
explanation.definitionFit: A racket is a din, and harsh discordant mixtures of sound are exactly that kind of noise.

clue.text: Artist requiring mostly brass and tin to start with

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: brass is British slang for cash

indicators.note: what something starts with is its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: A sculptor who works mainly in brass with a little tin at the beginning.
explanation.walkthrough: Brass and tin look like metals for a sculptor, but brass is slang for money, and in Britain tin is also slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: Claude Monet was the French Impressionist painter of the water lilies, so he is an example of an artist.

clue.text: Previous issue brought up I must introduce

indicators.note: to introduce is to come first, so one piece is placed ahead of the other

parts.note: the Roman numeral I is one

indicators.note: in a down entry, bringing letters up makes them read from bottom to top

parts.note: to issue is to send out or emit

explanation.surface: Someone insisting on raising an earlier matter at a meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Previous issue' looks like a back number of a magazine, but 'Previous' is the definition on its own and 'issue' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-time champion is a former one, so the hyphenated adjective means earlier or past.

clue.text: Chore that's beginning or ending on request

indicators.note: in a down entry, one thing on another sits directly above it
a word's beginning or ending is a single letter at one edge, and here either edge serves

parts.note: the word 'that' both starts and ends with the same letter
to ask is to request

explanation.surface: A household job that someone starts or finishes only when asked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That' begins and ends with T, so 'beginning or ending' gives the same letter either way.
explanation.definitionFit: A chore is a routine job to be done, and a task is a piece of work someone must carry out.

clue.text: Basic telly never thrown out

indicators.note: something thrown out is scattered in disarray, so the letters land in a new order

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A cheap old television set that nobody ever got round to dumping.
explanation.walkthrough: Telly is British for television. 'Basic telly' reads as one phrase, a no-frills set, but 'Basic' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An entry-level model is the simplest and cheapest version of a product, the one for beginners.

clue.text: Correspondence from someone who's shy?

parts.note: surface reading: a letter written by a timid person too bashful to speak
setter's reading: shy means short of money, as in 'a few pounds shy', so this is a written pledge to pay later

explanation.surface: A bashful person who writes letters rather than speaking up.
explanation.walkthrough: Shy has an older sense of lacking or short, as in 'ten pounds shy of the total'. Someone short of cash writes an IOU instead of paying.
explanation.definitionFit: The document is a signed written undertaking to pay a sum later, issued by a debtor who currently lacks funds.

clue.text: Strangely proper, sweet kids may exert such an influence

definitions.text: kids may exert such an influence
definitions.note: a descriptive clause standing for a noun phrase

indicators.note: done strangely means done in an odd, unfamiliar way, so the letters come out rearranged

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Oddly well-behaved, sweet-natured children can still get their way.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma makes 'proper, sweet kids' read as a description of children; 'kids' belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the leverage children have over parents by nagging them into buying things, a term used by marketers.

clue.text: Thieves with craving for ultimately breaking into post offices

indicators.note: breaking into somewhere means getting inside it, so letters go within others

parts.note: PO is the abbreviation for post office, made plural

indicators.note: going with something means being joined to it, so two pieces sit side by side

parts.note: to ache for something is to crave it

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, pointing at a word's final letter

parts.note: the final letter

explanation.surface: Burglars whose longing drives them to raid post offices.
explanation.walkthrough: The thieves breaking into post offices sound like the whole story; the break-in is the container instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Poachers take game or fish illegally from land they have no right to hunt on, a specific kind of thief.

clue.text: Exclusive hotel's abandoned southern Europeans

indicators.note: something abandoned is left behind, so it drops out of the word

parts.note: swish means smart, upmarket and exclusive
the abbreviation for south or southern
H is hotel in the phonetic alphabet; this is the letter removed

explanation.surface: Well-off southern Europeans have walked out of a smart hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests holidaymakers leaving a hotel; the hotel is only the letter H, and 'southern' is a letter too, not a description of Europeans.
explanation.definitionFit: The people of Switzerland are nationals of a country in central Europe, so they are Europeans.

clue.text: Evaluated drug said to suppress the onsets of intense migraines

parts.note: E is the drug ecstasy

indicators.note: to suppress is to hold something down and keep it in

parts.note: stated means said

indicators.note: onsets are beginnings, so the first letter of each word is taken

parts.note: the opening letters of both words

explanation.surface: A drug that was reviewed and reportedly holds off severe headaches.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a medical trial, with 'said' meaning reportedly; in the wordplay it is simply a synonym that gets split open.
explanation.definitionFit: To estimate is to judge or roughly calculate a value, which is what evaluating something means.

clue.text: Each serving of coffee maybe reported to recover energy

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so its sound counts, not its spelling

parts.note: each is per, and a cup is one serving of coffee

explanation.surface: A price list telling you the charge for every cup of coffee.
explanation.walkthrough: Coffee is also what makes you perk up, so the drink fits both halves of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means to become livelier or more cheerful after flagging, getting your energy back.

clue.text: With a time inside, escapee will then possibly make a fresh start

indicators.note: whatever is inside is put within something else, so these letters go in among the others
possibly signals one of several arrangements, so the letters may take a new order

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time
the letters to rearrange once the extra two are added
taken as written

explanation.surface: A convict who serves time and then breaks out hopes to begin a new life.
explanation.walkthrough: A and T go in among the letters of 'escapee will then', and the whole lot is rearranged. The prison story is the disguise: 'time inside' is not a sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to forget past mistakes and start again, from wiping chalk off a slate to leave it blank.

clue.text: State that is American at heart?

definitions.text: State that is American at heart?

parts.words: State that is American at heart?
parts.note: surface reading: a nation or region that is deeply American in character
setter's reading: the middle two letters of 'American' are RI, the postal abbreviation of this state

explanation.surface: Some place that, whatever it looks like, is truly American deep down.
explanation.walkthrough: The heart of AmeRIcan is RI, the standard abbreviation for this state, so the state literally sits in the middle of the word; the question mark flags the abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the smallest of the fifty US states, in New England, so it is literally an American state.

clue.text: Chat show host maybe at breaks changing celebs

indicators.note: what breaks something splits it apart and sits in the gap

parts.note: a conversion is a change from one thing to another
taken as written
the A-list is the top tier of celebrities

explanation.surface: A talk-show presenter who, during the ad breaks, swaps the famous guests around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaks' looks like commercial breaks in a TV show; it is the container instruction. The A-list is the top tier of famous people.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who talks fluently and entertainingly is good at chat, which a talk-show presenter is paid to be; 'maybe' marks an example.

clue.text: Extremely rare, specialist copy

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two outermost letters

parts.note: the first and last letters
a pro is a professional or expert

explanation.surface: An expert's replica of something exceptionally uncommon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely rare' reads as one phrase meaning very rare; 'Extremely' in fact picks out the edges of 'rare'.
explanation.definitionFit: A repro is short for a reproduction, a replica of an antique or artwork made to look like the original.

clue.text: Bad plonk, free

parts.note: to plonk something down is to put it down
to rid is to free, as in rid yourself of

explanation.surface: Terrible cheap wine given away for nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: Plonk is British slang for cheap wine, which is how the surface reads it, but here it is the verb meaning set down heavily.
explanation.definitionFit: Bad food has gone off, and putrid means rotten and decaying.

clue.text: Legally acquire scribes for an auditor

indicators.note: an auditor is a listener, so the words are judged by how they strike the ear

parts.note: to acquire is to buy, and to scribe is to write

explanation.surface: Obtaining writers lawfully on behalf of a financial inspector.
explanation.walkthrough: An auditor is usually an accountant checking books, which fits the business surface; here it is a hearer, from Latin audire.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means properly or according to what is just and rightful, close to lawfully.

clue.text: Flash, loose foreign police officer

parts.note: a flash is an instant, and a mo is a moment
to loose is to set free or untie

explanation.surface: A flamboyant, uninhibited policeman from abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flash' and 'loose' look like adjectives for a showy, lax officer; one is a noun meaning an instant and the other a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A Mountie is a member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, so to a British setter an officer from overseas.

clue.text: Recalled piece about old commercial deficit

indicators.note: to recall is to call back, so the letters run backwards
about means around, so the first word wraps round the next

parts.note: a part is a piece of something
aged means old

explanation.surface: Someone remembering a bit about an old advert.
explanation.walkthrough: The container is built first and only then read backwards. 'Old commercial' looks like a vintage advert, but 'commercial' belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The difference by which a country's imports exceed its exports is its trading shortfall in business terms.

clue.text: Resolved to relieve oil producer

indicators.note: to resolve can mean to break down into parts, which can then be reassembled differently

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone determined to help out an oil company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oil producer' suggests a petroleum firm, and 'Resolved' looks like determined; both are misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: The fruit of this Mediterranean plant is pressed to give cooking oil, so the plant produces oil.

clue.text: Classic Christmas movie crammed in fantastic ideas of winter

indicators.note: cramming something in means stuffing it inside something else
something fantastic is fanciful and unreal, so the letters are reimagined in a new order

parts.note: the letters to rearrange
crammed means packed full

explanation.surface: A favourite festive film packed with imaginative wintry notions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crammed' does double duty in the surface but gives FULL, which sits inside the rearranged 'ideas of winter'. The answer enumeration ignores the apostrophe.
explanation.definitionFit: Frank Capra's 1946 film with James Stewart is shown every December and is a staple of festive viewing.

clue.text: Palace staff worry endlessly about protecting carriage

indicators.note: to protect something is to wrap around and shield it
turning about means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards
without an end means the final letter is cut off

parts.note: stress is worry or anxiety
a van is a railway carriage for goods or luggage

explanation.surface: Royal household staff fretting over the state coach.
explanation.walkthrough: The carriage fits the palace picture as a royal coach; it is VAN, the old railway sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The people employed in a royal household to cook, clean and wait are its domestic staff.

clue.text: Area by train lines home to birds

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for area
via means by way of
RY is the abbreviation for railway

explanation.surface: A patch of land beside the railway tracks where birds nest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' reads as beside in the surface, but it gives VIA, meaning by way of.
explanation.definitionFit: An aviary is a large cage or enclosure built to keep birds in, so it is where they live.

clue.text: Flower seen in odd places in The Fens

indicators.note: odd places are the first, third, fifth and so on, so only those positions are read

parts.note: letters one, three, five and seven

explanation.surface: A bloom spotted in scattered spots across the flat marshland of eastern England.
explanation.walkthrough: The Fens are the low marshland of eastern England. A flower in crosswords is often a river, something that flows; the Tees runs through north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: A river is something that flows, so crossword setters call it a flower; this one reaches the North Sea at Middlesbrough.

clue.text: Bachelor drops ciggie: it's mental exhaustion

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for bachelor, as in BA
raindrops fall as rain
fag is British slang for a cigarette

explanation.surface: A single man gives up smoking and finds his mind worn out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drops' looks like a verb meaning quits; it is a noun, the drops that make up rain.
explanation.definitionFit: Brain fag is an old-fashioned term for tiredness of the mind from overwork, fag meaning weariness.

clue.text: Popular TV feature added to a magazine?

parts.note: something in is fashionable
a TV set

explanation.surface: A fashionable television section tacked into a magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a loose definition: an inset is an extra page or small panel set into a publication.
explanation.definitionFit: An inset is something inserted, such as an extra leaf in a publication or a small map within a larger one.

clue.text: Floods ripped through rock formations

indicators.note: going through something means passing inside it, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: tors are rocky outcrops on moorland hills
rent is an old past tense of rend, to tear

explanation.surface: Floodwater tore its way through rocky outcrops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Floods' looks like a verb here, but it is the plural noun, matching the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Torrents are rushing, violent streams of water, like a flood in full flow.

clue.text: Dismal days breed animosity in the end

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for day
to rear animals is to breed them

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the final letter

explanation.surface: Gloomy days eventually create bad feeling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dismal days' reads as a phrase, but only 'Dismal' is the definition; D is the abbreviation for day, here pluralised in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something gloomy, dull and depressing, so they are close synonyms.

clue.text: Neglected person recalled in novel

indicators.note: something novel is new, so the letters take a new form

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An overlooked figure who is remembered in a work of fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' pretends to be a book in which someone is remembered; it signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: From the fairy tale's overworked stepdaughter, the name is used for anyone or anything unfairly ignored or undervalued.

clue.text: Bread products also found in nice shops we supply

indicators.note: something found in a place lies inside it
read as the adverb of supple, it means flexibly, so the letters bend into a new shape

parts.note: the letters to rearrange
and means also, in addition

explanation.surface: A baker's claim that its loaves are stocked in pleasant shops it delivers to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' looks like the verb to provide; read as supple-ly it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A single slice of bread topped with a filling but no lid is something made from bread, so a bread product.

clue.text: Water container covered in kind of green waste

indicators.note: whatever is covered in something has that thing wrapped all round it

parts.note: sage is a soft grey-green colour
a ewer is a large water jug

explanation.surface: A water tank coated in some green sludge.
explanation.walkthrough: The green sludge makes 'waste' fit the scene; the green is a named shade, sage.
explanation.definitionFit: The word can mean the sewage carried away through drains, which is waste matter.

clue.text: In France, a proper source of drugs is not seized

parts.note: un is French for a
appropriate means proper or fitting

indicators.note: the source of something is where it starts, its first letter

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: A legitimate French drug supplier has escaped a police raid.
explanation.walkthrough: The drug-bust story suggests seizure by police; 'not seized' is simply the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To appropriate is to take for your own use, so something untouched by that has not been taken or claimed.

clue.text: Flower garden to some extent messed up when pruned

indicators.note: pruning cuts off the end growth, so the last letter goes

parts.note: in part means to some extent
erred means made a mistake

explanation.surface: A flower bed partly ruined after it was cut back.
explanation.walkthrough: The pruning fits the gardening picture perfectly, which hides that it only trims a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A parterre is a formal ornamental garden of flower beds laid out in a pattern, often beside a grand house.

clue.text: Permit curbing pub singer?

indicators.note: to curb something is to restrain it, holding it in

parts.note: to let is to permit
an inn is a pub

explanation.surface: A licensing rule to restrict performers in bars.
explanation.walkthrough: The pub singer looks like a performer at a karaoke night; the question mark warns the singer is a songbird.
explanation.definitionFit: The linnet is a small brown finch known for its twittering song, so it is a songbird.

clue.text: Work produced by digital artist?

parts.note: surface reading: an image made on a computer by a graphic designer
setter's reading: digits are fingers, so the artist applies colour by hand without a brush

explanation.walkthrough: Digital today suggests computers, but its root sense is to do with digits, the fingers.

clue.text: Thought advice restricts writers

parts.note: felt means thought or believed
a tip is a piece of advice
to pen something in is to confine it

explanation.surface: Considered guidance that limits authors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Restricts' looks like a container signal wrapping round 'writers', but it supplies a piece, and the writers are the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Pens are instruments for writing, so crossword setters call them writers; these have a fibre point.

clue.text: Takes steps to include official introductions

parts.note: to pace is to take steps
a ref is a referee, a match official

explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes steps' reads as takes action, but it is literal walking, and the official is a sports referee.
explanation.definitionFit: A preface is the opening section of a book in which the author introduces it to the reader.

clue.text: Silly preset mode restricting key measuring device

indicators.note: to restrict something is to confine it, holding it inside

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.walkthrough: 'Key' suggests a button on the device; it is a musical key, one of the letters A to G.
explanation.definitionFit: The dial on a car's dashboard gauges how fast the vehicle is travelling, so it measures speed.

clue.text: Where to find sailors working when lots of tourists are around

definitions.text: when lots of tourists are around

parts.note: the open ocean, far from land, is where sailors work
a machine that is on is working

explanation.surface: Ships are crewed and busy just when the holidaymakers turn up.
explanation.walkthrough: The break falls in a different place: HIGH SEAS plus ON, read as HIGH SEASON.
explanation.definitionFit: The busiest part of the year for holiday resorts, when visitors flock in and prices rise, is their peak period.

clue.text: An elite unit lacking one injured soldier

indicators.note: something injured is damaged and bent out of shape, so the letters are disordered
lacking something means going without it, so it is taken out

parts.note: the letters to rearrange
one is the Roman numeral I, the letter removed

explanation.surface: A crack army regiment short of one wounded trooper.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word fits a military report, so 'injured soldier' looks like one phrase; 'injured' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A lieutenant is a junior commissioned officer in the army, and so a soldier.

clue.text: Weird thing following everybody when it gets dark

indicators.note: something weird is strange and out of kilter, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters rearranged

all means everybody

explanation.surface: Something spooky comes after everyone once darkness falls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following' does two jobs: it abbreviates to F and it also places F ahead of ALL.

clue.text: Simple collection of data secures account

indicators.note: securing something means holding it fast inside

parts.note: a file is a set of stored data
AC is the abbreviation for account

explanation.surface: A basic database that protects someone's account details.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Simple collection of data' reads as one phrase; 'Simple' is the definition alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Facile means easily done or superficial, so it overlaps with easy or straightforward.

clue.text: Wow some vacuous fools

parts.note: gee is an exclamation of surprise

parts.note: the first and last letters

explanation.surface: An exclamation at how empty-headed certain idiots are.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some vacuous fools' reads as a group of airheads; 'vacuous' empties 'some' instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone a silly goose is an old insult for a foolish person, so geese are fools.

clue.text: Theatre backdrop packed up in crates, e.g. at storerooms

something packed is stowed inside a container, so the letters are tucked within
points to a run of letters lying within the words that follow

explanation.walkthrough: The theatre-storage picture is exact, which hides that the answer is sitting backwards in 'craTES EG AT Storerooms'.
explanation.definitionFit: The scenery and furniture built on the stage for a play form the physical setting behind the actors.

clue.text: Unyielding, dismissing son's argument

indicators.note: to dismiss is to send away, so a letter is removed

parts.note: stiff means rigid, not bending
S is the abbreviation for son, the letter removed

explanation.surface: A stubborn parent turning down their son's case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Son's argument' reads as the son's point of view, but the definition is 'argument' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiff is a petty quarrel between friends or lovers, a small squabble.

clue.text: Article kept in school: it's inside, alarmed

parts.note: the indefinite article

indicators.note: something inside is placed within the walls of another word

parts.note: in British boarding schools, being gated means being confined to the grounds as punishment
taken as written

clue.text: Marx perhaps had to leave when initially attacked with a weapon

parts.note: Harpo was one of the Marx Brothers

parts.note: to have is to own

clue.text: Heavy, heavy blow above American boxing ring

a ring is round, like the letter O

clue.text: Stop for something to drink

parts.note: a pier is a supporting pillar

clue.text: Report about heroin and another narcotic

clue.text: Live around a mile beyond the eastern edge of Liverpool, still

parts.note: to be is to exist or live

taken as written

parts.note: the final letter
